items.statement: In about 1 in 5 deaths blamed on mephedrone, tests after death found none of the drug.
items.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone, and in 25 of them tests found none. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one does not prove the drug caused the death.

items.statement: A negative fentanyl test strip means no other unexpected drugs are in the mix either.
items.why: A strip only shows whether fentanyl is there, not other drugs in the mix or how much. At one drug-checking service, 24 of 159 lab-checked samples held a newer benzo that none of the people who brought them expected.

items.statement: Cocaine cancels out alcohol, so someone who has had both isn't really drunk any more.
items.why: In small lab studies, known second-hand from one review, people felt only a little less drunk or no different, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about a tenth lower. Nobody tested driving, and about 4 in 100 drivers who died in crashes had both drugs in their blood.

items.statement: Pills don't help people stay away from heavy drinking.
items.why: One tablet, naltrexone, does a little: in dozens of trials about 46 in 100 people on it went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely, and most people in the trials also had counselling.

items.statement: Someone overdosing on meth goes quiet and sleepy, with slow breathing.
items.why: It can look like a body in overdrive: a racing heart, fast breathing, a very hot body, and a person who is very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality, though how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

items.statement: People who try weed are more likely to get hooked than people who try alcohol.
items.why: In an older US survey, about 9 in 100 people who had ever tried cannabis had been dependent at some point: fewer than for alcohol, tobacco, cocaine or heroin. Newer US figures are higher, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

items.statement: A positive urine test for weed shows the person used it in the past few days.
items.why: THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly: in two people who had used heavily, urine tests found cannabis for 67 and 93 days. A positive test doesn't show when or how much someone used.

items.statement: People who meet a 'being' on DMT mostly describe it as hostile.
items.why: Most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind, though 41 in 100 felt fear at some point. Only people who'd had such a meeting were asked, so this can't show how often it happens.

items.statement: Most people who met a 'being' on DMT later judged the meeting more real than everyday life.
items.why: Looking back, 65 in 100 of 2,561 adults said so, and 69 in 100 said the being gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.

items.statement: Among people who say a trip changed their beliefs, most afterwards thought plants could be conscious.
items.why: In a survey of 1,606 such people, 26 in 100 recalled thinking so before the trip and 61 in 100 after. They were looking back about 8 years on average, and superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

items.statement: In 2001 Portugal made it legal to have drugs for your own use.
items.why: Not legal: having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels instead of a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to between 5,000 and 5,500 a year.

items.statement: After Portugal decriminalised drugs in 2001, the share of adults using drugs in the past year barely changed.
items.why: Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100, but past-year use barely moved. Treatment and other help grew at the same time, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.

items.statement: MDMA with therapy has helped people with PTSD more than the same therapy with a dummy pill.
items.why: In two trials, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill. But in the trial that asked, most people knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

items.statement: In the days after a psychedelic like LSD or shrooms, people usually feel lower than before, like a comedown.
items.why: In most studies that checked, people reported less low mood and stress and more wellbeing a day to a month after, and none found mental health worse on average. Most were supported sessions with no dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause.

items.statement: Towns that trained more people to give naloxone, the overdose rescue medicine, had lower opioid death rates.
items.why: In Massachusetts, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower where more than 1 in 1,000 people were trained and given naloxone. It's a link, not proof: the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones.

items.statement: The old scare that LSD breaks your chromosomes turned out to be right.
items.why: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish. When 32 patients were tested before and after pure LSD there was no clear rise in damaged cells, though these were small studies of blood cells only.

items.statement: In a US test, about 1 in 5 CBD products bought online also contained THC.
items.why: Of 84 CBD oils, tinctures and vape liquids bought online in 2016, about 1 in 5 also held THC. No one took them, so the test can't say whether they cause a high or a positive drug test.

items.statement: Stopping benzos such as Xanax or Valium suddenly can bring on seizures.
items.why: Two expert reviews warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. They don't say how often: the only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.

items.statement: In lab tests, believing a drink was alcoholic made people drink more of it, whatever was really in the glass.
items.why: Men told their drink had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whether or not it did; real vodka made no clear difference. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

items.statement: In lab experiments, sexual arousal rose on average when people believed they'd drunk alcohol.
items.why: Across 36 experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more sexual arousal on average, though that varied a lot between studies. Mood and memory were changed by the alcohol itself, not the belief.

items.statement: In a lab test, people who often have caffeine were sleepier and slower without it than people who rarely do.
items.why: Skipping caffeine left them the sleepiest and slowest, and taking it only brought them level with people who rarely have it, no higher. People chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.

items.statement: Doctors have reported people having trouble walking after using laughing gas.
items.why: In doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide, 58 had trouble walking and 80 had numbness or tingling. Of the 100, 57 had used it for fun and 25 had it in surgery.

items.statement: Most people who die of a heroin overdose have no other drug in their body.
items.why: In older studies, no other drug was found in only 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose, and alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100. Finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.

items.statement: Ecstasy isn't a drug people become dependent on.
items.why: Some do: in US surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used it recently met the criteria for dependence, and more in some small groups. The checklists were made for other drugs, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy.

items.statement: Light weed smoking wears down lung function over the years, the way tobacco does.
items.why: In a 20-year study of about 5,000 adults, light cannabis smoking did not lower lung function; tobacco did. Smoking cannabis is still linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze, and too few people smoked it heavily for years to know what that does.

items.statement: The cough and wheeze linked to smoking weed tend to ease when people stop.
items.why: In two long-running studies, breathing symptoms eased in people who stopped. Many people also smoked tobacco, so the studies can't say how much of it comes from cannabis.

items.statement: Weed edibles are too mild to put a small child in hospital.
items.why: Of young children in US poison-centre calls about edibles, more than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital and 35 needed a breathing tube; no deaths were reported. Such calls rose about 15 times over from 2017 to 2021.

items.statement: People who have used LSD or magic mushrooms report more mental health problems than people who haven't.
items.why: But the gap vanished once their other drug use and life stress were counted: 98 in 100 had also used cannabis, for one. People were asked once, so this big US survey can't show whether these drugs cause or prevent problems.

items.statement: Some people who use weed regularly get bouts of severe vomiting.
items.why: In published cases, the bouts ended when people stopped cannabis: 62 of 64 who stopped got completely better, while the 21 who kept using did not. Nobody knows how common it is.

items.statement: Most people with weed-linked vomiting bouts found hot baths or showers eased them for a while.
items.why: That is from 211 published cases, though many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too. What ended the bouts, in the cases followed up, was stopping cannabis.

items.statement: Nicotine patches and gum don't actually help people quit smoking.
items.why: They help, modestly: after 6 months or more, about 16 in 100 had stopped with nicotine replacement, against 10 or 11 in 100 without. Many of the trials were paid for by drug companies.

items.statement: People drive about as well after weed as they do sober.
items.why: Across 80 lab studies, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly soon after THC than after a dummy. These are lab averages, so they can't give anyone a safe time to drive.

items.statement: When UK experts ranked 20 drugs by overall harm, heroin came out as the most harmful.
items.why: Alcohol came top, mostly for the harm it does to other people; for the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst. The scores are one panel's views, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.

items.statement: Tobacco probably kills more people than the 19 other drugs UK experts ranked, heroin and alcohol included, put together.
items.why: The ranking's own authors agreed it probably does. Yet tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose, because lung cancer was counted elsewhere in the scores.

items.statement: Most people who use kratom say they take it to get high.
items.why: In two US surveys, pain was the top reason, then anxiety or depression, and kratom's 'high' scored just 12 of 100. But the surveys reached people mostly through a pro-kratom group.

items.statement: Whether someone develops a drug problem comes down to their genes, not the home they grow up in.
items.why: Both are linked. In a Swedish study of adopted children, drug problems were about twice as common when a birth parent had one, and also more common in adoptive brothers and sisters, not related by birth, when the adopted child had one.

items.statement: In the famous 'Rat Park' experiments, rats living together left the morphine water alone.
items.why: They drank less of it than rats kept alone, but only in some tests; in one, they drank more. Two later attempts to repeat a Rat Park study did not find the same result, and rats aren't people.

items.statement: Sniffing solvents or sprays has been followed by sudden death in young people.
items.why: A 1969 US survey described 110 such deaths among people aged 11 to 23; in several, the person suddenly ran or panicked before collapsing. It counted deaths only, so it can't give the risk among everyone who used these products.

items.statement: Misleading news stories about fentanyl harming police by touch got far more Facebook shares than the corrections did.
items.why: US news articles coded as misinformation got about 450,000 Facebook shares; clear corrections got under 30,000. In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death.

items.statement: In one study, people who had quit heavy weed use still scored worse on thinking tests a year later.
items.why: People who had stopped heavy use for a year or more scored no differently on any test from people who had not used. Studies of people 3 to 8 weeks after stopping disagree, and researchers read the evidence in opposite ways.

items.statement: People who use weed several days a week are less motivated than people who have barely tried it.
items.why: In a London study, people using cannabis about 4 days a week felt no less motivated and were as willing to work for sweets. It was a one-time snapshot, so it can't show what years of heavy daily use do.

items.statement: Teenagers in London reported less motivation than adults, whether or not they used weed.
items.why: Scores differed more by age than by cannabis use: teens reported less motivation and less pleasure than adults either way. People were tested with questionnaires and lab tasks, not at school or work.

items.statement: Alcohol withdrawal is unpleasant, but it doesn't cause seizures.
items.why: It can: in old trials, about 8 in 100 people going through alcohol withdrawal on dummy pills had a seizure. With calming medicines called benzodiazepines, about 1 in 100 did.

items.statement: When people stop long-term heavy drinking, their sleep is back to normal within a few days.
items.why: In sleep-lab studies, many slept badly for weeks or months after stopping, with less deep sleep. This comes second-hand from one review that did not check how good the studies were.

items.statement: People off cocaine for several months scored close to people who don't use it on memory and attention tests.
items.why: In 5 studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months, scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

items.statement: On some brain scans, parts of the brain looked larger, not smaller, in people who used meth.
items.why: Studies disagree: soon after stopping, some brain areas looked smaller, while other studies found some larger. The groups also differed in smoking, schooling and low mood, and some differences may not last.

items.statement: Before it was banned in 1985, MDMA was used by some US therapists in talking therapy.
items.why: A few dozen US therapists used it and reported good results, but the reports of the time were not designed well enough to show whether it helped. After the ban, research applications were blocked for years.

items.statement: The link between weed and car crashes gets much smaller once drivers' drinking is taken into account.
items.why: Studies that allowed for alcohol found drivers with cannabis in a test had 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash; studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times. Either way, cannabis in a test was linked to more crashes.

items.statement: Drinking water between alcoholic drinks stops a hangover.
items.why: In one small test, 13 men felt no better the next morning when they had water between drinks than when they drank the same sake without it. With so few men, a small benefit can't be ruled out.

items.statement: Drinking beer before wine gives a milder hangover than wine before beer.
items.why: When young adults drank beer and wine in both orders on different days, the hangover was about the same. Only one kind of beer and one white wine were tested.

items.statement: In their first weeks off cocaine, people felt they slept better while sleep-lab machines showed them sleeping worse.
items.why: By the third week, machines showed they took longer to fall asleep and slept less, yet their own ratings of sleep got better. It's one small study of 20 people in a hospital unit.

items.statement: Caffeine can keep people awake longer in the night without them noticing.
items.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made time awake in the night longer and sleep lighter. Yet in five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

items.statement: Most people who have had a drinking problem have not looked for treatment or help.
items.why: In a US survey, about 20 in 100 people who had ever had alcohol use disorder said they had looked for help, and about 35 in 100 of those with a severe one. People reported this themselves, and the survey left out most people in treatment.

items.statement: When weed use in the UK soared after the 1970s, hospital stays for schizophrenia climbed with it.
items.why: A review says cannabis use rose at least tenfold while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise. But studies disagree: psychosis did become more common in people born more recently in south-east London and Zurich.

items.statement: Since weed usually comes first, it must be what leads people on to other illegal drugs.
items.why: Coming first doesn't prove it leads on: a computer model in which cannabis did nothing still produced the same pattern. Whether cannabis plays any part is still not known, and experts disagree.

items.statement: In one study, older people who took the most benzos got dementia about as often as those who took none.
items.why: About 3 in 100 a year got dementia either way, in a Seattle study that tested 3,434 older people. Quebec health records did link long use to Alzheimer's, but early dementia can bring the worry and poor sleep that lead to the pills.

items.statement: After Vancouver opened a supervised injection site, overdose deaths in the streets around it went up.
items.why: Within 500 metres they fell by about a third, against about a tenth elsewhere in the city. It's one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, so this doesn't prove the site was the reason.
